exam: What clinical feature distinguishes enteric fever from malaria? — Relative bradycardia (Faget’s sign) with a step‑ladder fever pattern.
A patient on ceftriaxone remains febrile after 5 days; what is your next step? — Review culture sensitivity, consider resistant strain, and switch to azithromycin if susceptibility allows.
How would you manage a suspected intestinal perforation in a low‑resource hospital? — Stabilise with IV fluids, give broad‑spectrum antibiotics, arrange urgent transfer for surgery.
Why is fluoroquinolone avoidance recommended in East Africa? — High rates of nalidixic‑acid and ciprofloxacin resistance make them unreliable.
Explain the interpretation of a four‑fold rise in Widal titres. — Suggests recent infection but must be correlated with clinical picture due to endemic baseline titres.
What vaccination strategy reduces community incidence of enteric fever? — Single‑dose Typhoid Conjugate Vaccine for children >6 months and high‑risk adults, with catch‑up campaigns.
ai.title: Enteric (Typhoid) Fever
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Enteric fever is a systemic infection caused by Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi, presenting with prolonged fever, relative bradycardia and possible intestinal complications. Diagnosis relies on blood culture and clinical pattern, while management combines appropriate antibiotics and supportive care.

b: Diagnosis requires isolation of the organism from blood (first week) or stool/urine (later weeks).
In low‑resource settings, a positive Widal test may support the diagnosis but is not definitive.
sections.p: Enteric fever is a febrile illness due to Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi or Paratyphi, characterised by bacteremia without an initial focal source.

b: Uncomplicated: fever, malaise, rose spots, no organ dysfunction.
Complicated: intestinal perforation, hemorrhage, encephalopathy, or severe sepsis.
sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical course and complications rather than a formal stage system.

b: S. Typhi – most common worldwide.
S. Paratyphi A – increasingly common in parts of Asia and Africa.
Co‑infection with HIV or malaria can worsen outcome.
sections.p: The disease is acquired by ingestion of contaminated food or water.

b: Headache, constipation or diarrhoea, and mild hepatosplenomegaly.
In children, irritability and failure to thrive may dominate.
sections.p: Typical presentation is a step‑ladder rise in temperature over 5‑7 days, relative bradycardia (Faget’s sign), abdominal discomfort and faint rose‑coloured macules on trunk.

t.b: Confirms pathogen; positive culture = definitive diagnosis.
Detects carrier state; positive = ongoing shedding.
Assesses anti‑O and anti‑H titres; a four‑fold rise suggests infection but false‑positives are common.
Leukopenia with left shift is typical; if unavailable, rely on clinical picture.
Mild transaminase rise supports systemic infection; severe rise may signal hepatic involvement.

b: Intestinal perforation – sudden abdominal pain, peritonitis.
Gastrointestinal bleeding – melena or hematemesis.
Encephalopathy – altered mental status, seizures.
Septic shock – hypotension, cold clammy skin.
sections.p: Complications develop after the first week and carry high mortality if untreated.

b: First‑line antibiotics: ceftriaxone or azithromycin – chosen for activity against resistant strains and good tissue penetration.
Avoid fluoroquinolones where high resistance is documented (e.g., East Africa).
If perforation suspected, arrange urgent surgical assessment.
Fluid resuscitation, antipyretics, and nutritional support are essential.
sections.p: Treat the organism promptly and support organ function.

b: Repeat blood culture at day 14 if fever persists.
Screen household contacts; treat carriers with oral ciprofloxacin for 4 weeks if susceptible.
Typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) given to children >6 months and high‑risk adults.
sections.p: Monitor for relapse and carriage; vaccinate at-risk populations.

b: Malaria – periodic fever, haemolysis; malaria smear distinguishes.
Brucellosis – undulating fever, hepatosplenomegaly; serology helps.
Acute HIV seroconversion – rash, lymphadenopathy; HIV test required.
sections.p: Several febrile illnesses mimic enteric fever in low‑resource settings.

b: Widal test may be positive from prior vaccination or endemic exposure.
Blood cultures can be negative after antibiotics; consider stool culture or PCR if available.
sections.p: Certain tests have limited reliability in endemic areas.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden abdominal pain with guarding (possible perforation)
Vomiting of blood or black stools
